parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones the organiser of a city half-marathon to enter the race.
script: Good morning, Riverbend Half-Marathon entries line, Rebecca speaking.
Oh, hello. I'd like to enter the half-marathon, please. I hope I'm not too late.
Not at all. Entries stay open for another two weeks, so you're fine. I can take your details over the phone if you like.
Lovely. Let's start with your surname.
Sorry, was that a K or a Q in the middle?
A Q, like queen. It's a Swedish name. My grandfather came over in the nineteen fifties and everybody has been getting it wrong ever since.
Well, I've got it now. L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T. And your address?
Let me think. It's NR2 9LP. No, sorry, that's my old flat. The new one is NR2 9LT.
NR2 9LT. Got it. And a contact number?
No, 365. Three, six, five at the end.
Sorry about that. 07911 428 365. Right, now, I think you've already seen that the race is on Sunday 12 April?
Yes, that's what's in my diary.
Ah, I think you may be thinking of the ten kilometre fun run. That takes place on the twelfth. The half-marathon is the following weekend, so Sunday 19 April.
Oh, thank goodness you said. I'd have turned up a week early.

It happens quite often. Now, the elite runners set off at 9.00, but everybody else starts at 9.30, so that's your time. We ask people to be in the start area by 9.00 so that we can get everyone lined up.
That's fine. I'm not an elite runner, believe me. I'm just hoping to finish.

That's what most of us say. Now, the entry fee. If you enter online it's 30 pounds, but because we're taking your entry by phone, it's 35 pounds. After the first of April it goes up to 40 pounds, so you're in good time.
35 pounds is no problem. Can I pay by card?
Of course. I'll send you a secure link by text in a moment. Every entrant gets a race T-shirt, so what size would you like? We do small, medium, large and extra large.
I'm usually a large, but the shirt from the last race I did came up very big. I think medium would be safer.
Medium it is. Our shirts are a fairly generous cut, so that sounds wise.
Can I ask where the money goes? I like to know that I'm helping somebody.
Of course. Last year the profit went to the lifeboat service, but this year it's all going to the Riverside Hospice. They look after patients from all over the county, so we're very pleased.
That's a good cause. I might try to raise a bit of sponsorship for them as well.

They'd be delighted. I'll include a sponsorship form in your pack. Which brings me to the pack itself. Last year you collected it from the Sports Hall at the university, but that's being repaired, so this year it's the Corn Exchange in the city centre, on Friday afternoon from 2 until 7, or on the Saturday morning.
The Corn Exchange. Friday will suit me best, I think. Do I need to bring anything?
Yes. Your confirmation email is helpful, but what we really need is photo ID. A passport or a driving licence is fine. A bank card isn't enough, I'm afraid.
My driving licence is at my mother's house at the moment, so I'll bring my passport.
That's perfect. Is there anything else I can help you with?
No, I think that's everything. Thank you very much, Rebecca.
You're very welcome, Callum. Good luck with the training, and we'll see you in April.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A coordinator briefs volunteers on the day before a city marathon.
script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you so much for coming. For those who haven't met me, I'm Dana Whitfield, and I'm the volunteer coordinator for this year's Harbour City Marathon. Let's start with the headline news. We have 320 of you signed up, which is a record, and I want you to know that without you this event simply couldn't happen.

First, the practical details. The email you received said to report at 6 o'clock on race morning. That has changed, I'm afraid. The police are closing the main roads earlier than planned, so please be at the volunteer tent by 5.30. I know that's early, but the first wave of runners sets off at 8, and everything has to be ready well before then. If you're coming from outside the city, please do allow extra time.

When you arrive, you'll collect a bright yellow jacket, which you must wear all day so that runners and officials can spot you. Please hand it back at the tent when you've finished. People often ask whether there's a free entry to next year's race. There is, but only for volunteers who help at three events in a row, so that's something to think about for the future. What every volunteer does get is a voucher for lunch at the food stalls, which you can use once your shift is over.

Now, a word about parking, because it causes more complaints than anything else. Normally people leave their cars along Embankment Road, but that will be closed completely. The stadium car park is reserved for runners and their families. So we've arranged for you to use the university car park on Mill Street. It's about a ten-minute walk from the start area, and it's free as long as you show your volunteer badge at the barrier.

Let's turn to the course itself. There are twelve water stations along the route, and many of you will be working at one of them. People assume that the biggest problem will be queues, but runners are surprisingly polite, and queues sort themselves out. They also assume we might run out of cups, but we've ordered 60,000, which should be plenty. The real problem is what happens afterwards. Hundreds of used cups land on the road, and wet plastic is extremely slippery. A runner who skids can bring down the people behind, so somebody needs to sweep the road every few minutes.

Now, safety, which is the most important thing I'll say today. If you see a runner in trouble, perhaps someone who has collapsed, or who seems confused, your first instinct will be to help them to the side of the road. Please don't. Stay with them, and call the medical number that's printed on the back of your badge. The first aid team has bicycles, and they'll reach you within a few minutes. And please don't offer them water or try to move them. Leave that to the professionals.
Right, let me confirm who is doing what. I'll go through the team leaders now, and you'll find all the details on the sheet you were given at the door.

Marcus, you're leading the baggage team. You'll be in the big tent behind the start line, looking after runners' bags until they come back. Priyanka, you'll be in charge of the water station at the ten kilometre mark. It's the busiest one, because it's where most people start to flag.

Tom, I originally put you with the first aid team, but I've just remembered that your certificate ran out in March, so I've moved you. You'll be at the finish line, handing out medals and foil blankets. Elena, you asked for something more active, so you'll be a course marshal on Bridge Street, making sure that nobody wanders across the road. And Joseph, you'll run the registration desk, where late entrants collect their numbers. That's a tricky job, so thank you for taking it on.

Finally, a quick word about the weather. The forecast says it will be cool and dry, but it's likely to be windy by the river, so wear layers. You'll be standing for hours, and it's surprising how cold you get when everyone else is running. There'll be hot drinks at the volunteer tent, and you'll each have a half-hour break. Please make sure you take it.

That's everything from me. I'll be here for the next twenty minutes if you have questions, and then we'll walk the route together. Thank you again, and I'm looking forward to seeing you all on Sunday.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss a statistics assignment on house prices.
script: Jack, have you got a minute? I'd like to go over our house prices assignment before we see Dr Marsh on Friday.
Sure. Did you manage to download the full dataset in the end?
I did, yes. Do you remember why we chose house prices in the first place? I've completely forgotten.

Well, Dr Marsh gave us three datasets to choose from, and she said she didn't mind which one we picked. The transport one looked far too big, and the bird survey seemed rather dull. I think it was mostly because it's our own city, so we have a feeling for whether the results make sense.
That's right. If a district looks cheap, we'd probably know if there was something odd about it.
Exactly. And downloading it wasn't hard, but that wasn't what decided it.
The only real problem is that the file has some gaps. The prices for two districts are missing for 2016, which is annoying.
Yes, but I'd rather work with that than go out and collect new data. There are plenty of other variables, but we only need about four of them, so it isn't too much to cope with.

True. And it's recent enough, up to last year, so we can't complain about that. Now, there's something else. Look at this one sale in Kingsmead. It's 4.2 million pounds, which is ten times the next highest price.
Wow. That's got to be a mistake. I suggest we simply delete it.
I'm not sure we should. I checked, and it's a real sale. A whole country house, apparently. If we delete it, we're hiding something that really happened.
Good point. We could replace it with an estimate, I suppose.
That would be even worse, because we'd be inventing a number. I think we keep it in and say in the report that it's unusual. Dr Marsh likes it when students comment on odd results.
All right, I'm happy with that. We keep it and explain it.
Good. Now, did you read her comments on our draft?
I did. I thought she'd say the introduction was far too long, but she didn't.
No, the length was fine. And she didn't complain about the references, either. Her point was that we never say what we are actually trying to find out. The aim is too vague.
So we need one clear sentence at the start. I'll have a go at that. Who does what before Friday?
I'll produce all the graphs tonight, if you write the method section. And could you check the references as well? I always get those wrong.
No problem. Right, let's decide what to use in each part of the report. Starting with the typical price across the whole city. I'd use the mean, because that's what everyone expects.
I wouldn't. The mean will be dragged up by that Kingsmead sale. The median is much safer, because it isn't affected by one extreme value.
Fair enough, the median. Then for the second section, how prices have changed over the last ten years, I think a line graph is the obvious choice.

Agreed. One line for the whole city, otherwise it will look like spaghetti. Then for the relationship between floor area and price, we need a scatter graph. You can see at a glance whether bigger houses cost more.
And then we'd want to put a single figure on how strong that relationship is. That would be the correlation coefficient.
Yes. And finally, for the last section, we'll show how much the districts differ. Simply the gap between the cheapest district and the most expensive one, so the range.
Perfect. That gives us a nice, clear structure. Shall we meet in the library tomorrow to put it all together?

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the history of the postal service.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to look at something so familiar that we rarely stop to think about it: the postal service. Every time you drop a card into a letterbox, you're using a system that took about two and a half thousand years to develop, and I'd like to trace some of the main steps in that story.

Let's begin with the earliest organised system that we know much about, which belonged to the Persian kings. They built a network of roads and, along those roads, relay stations placed roughly a day's ride apart. A rider would gallop from one station to the next, hand over the message and, crucially, change his horses. A fresh animal meant that the message never slowed down, and a royal order could cross an enormous empire in a matter of days instead of months.

The Romans copied the idea and called their version the cursus publicus. It was extremely efficient, but there was an important limit. It carried only official messages: orders from the emperor, reports from the army and so on. Private individuals had no right to use it. If an ordinary Roman wanted to send a letter to his brother in another province, he had to rely on friends travelling in the right direction, or, more often, on merchants, who were generally happy to carry a letter if you gave them a small payment.

After the Roman Empire collapsed, the postal system in Western Europe fell apart as well. For several centuries there was nothing that we would recognise as a public service. What took its place was a patchwork. In the medieval period, monasteries ran their own messengers, so that the monks could stay in touch with other houses, and so did the universities. These were closed networks, though, designed for members only.

The next big development came in the sixteenth century, and it came from a family rather than from a government. The Taxis family, who originally came from northern Italy, organised relays of riders linking cities across Europe. Their service carried official letters for the Habsburg rulers, but it also carried letters for anyone who was willing to pay. That is the beginning of the idea that the post is a service for the public. There was one major difference from today, however. It wasn't the sender who paid for a letter in those days, but the recipient. And that created an obvious problem, because people sometimes refused to accept the letter, and the courier would have to carry it all the way back.

In Britain, a royal postal service was opened to the public in 1635 by Charles the First. Prices were complicated. A letter was charged according to the number of sheets of paper, which is why people wrote on both sides and used the thinnest paper they could find, and also according to the distance it travelled. A letter from London to Edinburgh cost a great deal more than one to a neighbouring town, and the clerks needed to work out the price for each letter individually.

By the 1830s the system was slow and expensive, and that's when a schoolteacher named Rowland Hill made a proposal that changed everything. In 1837 he argued that the real cost of carrying a letter was tiny compared with the cost of calculating and collecting the charge. So he suggested a uniform rate of one penny for any letter, however far it went. And, even more radically, he proposed that the sender should pay in advance. In 1840 this led to the first adhesive postage stamp, the famous Penny Black. Within a few years, the number of letters posted in Britain had more than doubled.

The other great force in the nineteenth century was the railway. Once trains began to link the major cities, mail could be moved at a speed that had been impossible before. Even more cleverly, the Post Office began to fit out carriages as moving sorting offices, so that letters were sorted on trains during the journey and were ready for delivery the moment the train arrived.

The twentieth century brought more changes: air mail, postcodes and machines that could read addresses. But since about the year 2000 the volume of ordinary letters has fallen steadily in most countries, mainly because of email, which has taken over most personal and business correspondence.

That might sound like the end of the story, but it isn't. Postal services are now busier than ever with parcels, because of the growth in online shopping. Many post offices have had to reinvent themselves as parcel companies, with vans, lockers and tracking apps. So the old principle of the Persian relay stations, getting a package from one point to another as fast as possible, lives on, just in a very different form. Thank you, and I'll take any questions now.

passages.title: The Silk Road: a network of ideas
paras: A  The name 'Silk Road' would have puzzled the people who actually used it. It was coined only in 1877, by a German geographer who wanted a label for the ancient trading routes that linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean, and it stuck because it was memorable. Yet it is misleading in two ways. There was never a single road: the name covers a shifting web of tracks, mountain passes and river crossings that threaded through the deserts and highlands of Central Asia for some 1,500 years. And silk, though prized in Rome and Persia, was only one commodity among many. Jade, spices, glassware, horses, furs, precious metals and slaves all moved along the same routes, and so, more quietly, did beliefs, inventions and stories. Many historians now prefer to think of the Silk Road as a network of ideas as much as a channel of trade.

B  Few travellers ever covered the whole distance. A cargo of silk leaving a Chinese city would change hands many times, with each merchant selling it on at a profit to the next, and by the time it reached the Mediterranean its price had multiplied several times over. The most successful middlemen were the Sogdians, whose homeland lay in what is now Uzbekistan. From the fourth century onwards their trading colonies stretched from Samarkand to the borders of China, and their language became the common tongue of commerce along the routes, much as English is in international business today. Merchants rested at oasis towns, where they stayed in fortified inns known as caravanserai, bargained for fresh camels and exchanged news. These settlements grew wealthy, and some, including Samarkand and Kashgar, became centres of learning as well as markets.

C  Religion travelled with the traders. Buddhism, which began in northern India, reached China during the first century AD, carried partly by merchants who funded monasteries along the way in the hope of spiritual protection on dangerous journeys. Monks followed, translating scriptures into Chinese and establishing communities in the oasis towns. At Dunhuang, on the edge of the Gobi Desert, thousands of manuscripts were sealed inside a cave library, where they survived for centuries; they include texts in languages that few scholars can read today. Art shows the same mingling of cultures. In the region of Gandhara, sculptors who had inherited a Greek tradition, left behind by the armies of Alexander the Great, carved images of the Buddha with wavy hair and flowing robes that look more like Mediterranean statues than Indian ones.

D  Technology also moved, sometimes with dramatic consequences. Paper, invented in China, was unknown in the Islamic world until the eighth century, when, according to tradition, Chinese prisoners taught the craft in Samarkand. Within a few generations paper mills were operating in Baghdad, and the cheap new material helped to make the great libraries of the age possible. Printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass eventually followed similar paths westward. Traffic in the opposite direction was just as significant. China acquired powerful horses from the Ferghana valley, as well as grapes, walnuts and alfalfa, and new musical instruments such as the lute entered Chinese courts from Persia. Even the ordinary diet of the towns along the routes was transformed by crops that had originated thousands of kilometres away.

E  Not every exchange was welcome. The routes that carried ideas also carried disease, and many scholars believe that the plague which devastated Europe in the fourteenth century travelled along them, although the exact path remains disputed. In the thirteenth century, however, the Mongol Empire, which at its height controlled most of the land between China and eastern Europe, imposed a rare period of security. Merchants carrying a metal tablet of authority could cross thousands of kilometres with little fear of bandits, and travellers such as the Venetian Marco Polo returned home with accounts that astonished their readers. Historians sometimes call this era the Mongol Peace, and it was probably the busiest period in the whole history of the routes.

F  The decline of the network is often blamed on the Ottoman Empire, which supposedly closed the overland routes to European merchants in the fifteenth century and forced them to look for a way round by sea. Recent research suggests that this story is mistaken. Ottoman rulers had every reason to keep the trade flowing, because they taxed it. The real change was economic: ships had become larger and more reliable, and carrying goods by sea was far cheaper than moving them by camel across thousands of kilometres of desert. Overland trade did not vanish overnight, and some towns continued to prosper for generations, but its role as the main link between civilisations slowly faded.

G  Today the old routes attract archaeologists, tourists and politicians alike. In 2014 a section of the network linking China with Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, and several governments have launched modern infrastructure projects that borrow the historic name. Whether or not such schemes succeed, the original Silk Road offers a lasting lesson: that cultures are rarely isolated, and that much of what any society considers its own has, at some point, arrived from somewhere else. A single bolt of silk may have made a merchant's fortune, but it was the stories, faiths and skills travelling in his baggage that changed the world.

passages.title: Flavour: the partnership of taste and smell
paras: A  Ask most people what the tongue does and they will say that it tastes. Ask what the nose does and they will say that it smells. The reality is that flavour, the sensation we describe when we say a dish is delicious, is built from both senses working together, with contributions from touch, temperature and even sound. Scientists define taste narrowly as what the tongue itself can detect: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, the savoury quality found in foods such as mushrooms, aged cheese and meat broth. Everything else that we think of as the flavour of strawberries, coffee or roast chicken comes from the nose.

B  Our confusion on this point has a long history. For most of the twentieth century, school textbooks showed a 'map' of the tongue, with sweetness detected at the tip, bitterness at the back, and sour and salty tastes along the sides. The map originated in a misreading of a German thesis published in 1901, and it is wrong. Receptors for all five tastes are scattered across the whole tongue, as well as on the palate and in the throat, although some areas are slightly more sensitive to certain substances than others. The map survived in classrooms for decades because it was simple, neat and rarely tested, and many adults still believe in it.

C  Smell is far more complex. Whereas taste relies on just a handful of receptor types, the human nose contains around 400 different kinds of olfactory receptor, which, working in combination, can distinguish an enormous range of odours; estimates once put the number at 10,000, and a controversial study suggested a trillion. When we chew, aromas released from the food travel from the back of the mouth up into the nasal cavity. This 'retronasal' route explains why food seems bland when we have a cold. The tongue still reports sweetness or saltiness, but the nose, blocked, cannot supply the rest. A well-known demonstration shows the effect: with the nose pinched shut, people often cannot tell a piece of apple from a piece of raw potato until they let go.

D  People also differ in how sharply they experience taste. About a quarter of the population are classed as 'supertasters', who have more taste buds than average and find bitter substances such as black coffee, dark chocolate and some vegetables unpleasantly strong. Another quarter are 'non-tasters', who are largely indifferent to these flavours, and the rest fall in between. Genetics explains part of the difference, but not all of it. Experience matters, too. Babies are born with a liking for sweetness and a dislike of bitterness, which probably helped our ancestors to avoid poisons, but later preferences are learnt. Some studies suggest that flavours from a mother's diet pass into amniotic fluid and breast milk, so that children whose mothers ate carrots during pregnancy may accept carrots more readily.

E  Smell has a unique connection to emotion and memory. Signals from the nose travel to the olfactory bulb, which lies close to the amygdala and the hippocampus, two regions involved in emotion and memory; information from the other senses is routed through a relay station in the brain first. This may explain why a whiff of sun cream can bring back a childhood holiday with startling vividness. It also helps to explain why losing the sense of smell, which has affected millions of people through viral infections and, more gradually, through ageing, is more than an inconvenience. Many sufferers report that food becomes joyless, and some lose their appetite and a good deal of weight. Others fail to notice smoke or spoiled food, which creates real dangers, and a number develop depression.

F  Not all the sensations we call flavour belong to taste or smell at all. The burn of a chilli pepper, the cooling effect of mint and the tingle of fizzy water are detected by nerves in the mouth that respond to pain, temperature and touch, rather than by taste buds. Texture matters, too: the same flavour can seem pleasant in a smooth sauce and unappealing in a gritty one. Even hearing plays a part. Food manufacturers have long exploited such findings. Aroma compounds are added to products to make them smell richer, and the crunch of a crisp is carefully engineered, because experiments show that louder crunches make the same snack seem fresher.

G  Researchers are now exploring how knowledge of taste and smell could help people whose appetite has fallen, such as the elderly and the seriously ill. Adding stronger flavours to hospital meals, for example, has been shown to increase how much patients eat, and a team in one university is testing 'scent training', in which people recovering from smell loss sniff four familiar odours twice a day for several months. The early results are encouraging. The work is a reminder that, in eating as in much of life, the senses do not operate as separate channels but as a team.

passages.title: The paradox of labour-saving devices
paras: A  In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that, within a century, technology would have advanced so far that his grandchildren would work no more than fifteen hours a week. We are now close to that deadline, and the prediction looks absurd. Households own washing machines, dishwashers, robot vacuum cleaners and a tide of other devices that once seemed miraculous, yet most adults report feeling busier than their grandparents ever did. I want to argue that this paradox is not a sign that technology has failed, nor evidence that people are foolish, but a consequence of something we rarely examine: what we choose to do with the time that machines give back.

B  Historians of domestic life uncovered the paradox decades ago. When electric appliances spread through North American and European homes between the 1920s and the 1960s, advertisers promised liberation from drudgery. Surveys of how households actually spent their time told a different story. Women who owned washing machines did not spend noticeably fewer hours on housework than women who did not. Part of the reason is that the work itself changed. Once laundry no longer meant a day of carrying water and scrubbing by hand, families changed their clothes more often, expected sheets to be washed weekly rather than monthly, and treated a stain as a failure rather than a fact of life. The machine reduced the effort of each task but multiplied the number of tasks. Many commentators take this as proof that appliances were a swindle. I think that conclusion is too hasty. Clothes were cleaner, kitchens safer and children healthier; what people gained was not leisure but a higher standard of living.

C  The same pattern appears at work. Word processors made documents easy to revise, so we now revise them endlessly. Email removed the delay of the postal system, so we are expected to reply within the hour. Spreadsheets can model a hundred scenarios in the time it once took to calculate one, and managers duly ask for a hundred. Economists have a name for the general principle: when a resource becomes cheaper to use, people tend to use more of it, sometimes so much more that total consumption rises. Nineteenth-century observers noticed it with coal, as more efficient engines led to more coal being burnt, not less. Time appears to behave in the same way. When tasks become quicker, we do not bank the saving; we fill the gap with further tasks.

D  It is tempting to blame employers, and some blame is deserved. Competitive pressure ensures that a firm whose staff become twice as productive is unlikely to send them home at lunchtime; it will expect twice as much output. But this explanation is incomplete, because the pattern also holds in areas where nobody is giving us orders. Parents with more labour-saving equipment still take on more of their children's activities, driving them to more clubs and supervising homework more closely than previous generations did. Nobody forces such choices on them. They flow from rising expectations of what a good parent, a good employee or a good host ought to achieve, and expectations, unlike dishwashers, have no built-in limit.

E  If so, the usual remedies are unlikely to work. Productivity gurus advise us to automate more, delegate more and cut distractions, but each new technique simply raises the ceiling of what we think we can accomplish. Others call for governments to legislate for shorter working weeks. This may help, and several experiments with four-day weeks have reported encouraging results, but a rule imposed from outside does not alter the habit of mind that fills any freed hours with fresh obligations. A teacher who is given Fridays off may well spend them marking. I do not believe that shorter hours can succeed on their own; they must be accompanied by a change in how we value our own time.

F  What might such a change look like? First, we could decide in advance what the time saved is for, instead of leaving it to be absorbed. A family that buys a dishwasher might agree that the half hour recovered each evening is spent together and not on more chores. Second, we could be more sceptical of the standards that advertisers and colleagues set. Much of what we call necessity is only habit; the weekly ironing of bed linen, for instance, is a custom rather than a requirement. Third, we should accept that doing less is sometimes an achievement. None of this is easy, and I do not claim that it will reverse the trend overnight. But Keynes' mistake was not about technology; it was about human nature. The machines kept their side of the bargain. It is we who have not yet learnt to take the reward.
